title: GPU Clocking & KV Cache Tuning — Ops Cheatsheet and Experiment Log
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact operational cheat sheet and experimental log for GPU clocking and KV cache tuning across our primary inference fleet (NVIDIA A100/H100, NVIDIA L4, AMD MI300). It is intentionally pragmatic: quick checks, safe defaults, measurement recipes, and escalation/rollback steps for on-call and perf engineers. Use this as the first-stop when investigating latency regressions or cost-vs-latency tuning windows.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to production inference nodes and staging clusters used for rollout testing.
- Focus is on per-instance clocking/power cap knobs, kernel selection hints, and KV cache sizing/eviction behaviors that materially change per-token latency and throughput.
- Doesn’t replace firmware/BIOS guidance from vendors. Tie any persistent changes to vendor recommendations and SRE change control.

High-level notes on devices (practical differences):
- A100 (PCIe/400GB): strong FP16/TF32 perf; relatively high sustained power budget; good for long-context models where KV cache fits on device memory. Prefers sustained clocking profiles (avoid aggressive turbo without thermal headroom).
- H100: higher peak perf, larger boost headroom; transient turbo is powerful but thermal/VRM throttling shows up quickly under microbursts. Lower tolerance for long sustained max clocks unless cooling is provisioned.
- L4: power-efficient, lower single-stream latency cost; limited memory for KV cache on long contexts — gate batching carefully and prefer small per-request KV residency.
- MI300: different memory architecture (HBM + chiplet); kernel availability differs (we use ROCm builds). Quantization fallback behaviors and kernel codepaths must be validated; clock/power controls are coarser.

Quick safe defaults (start here for triage):
- A100: set power cap to 300W for 80GB models, 250W for 40GB variants if thermal headroom limited. Set sustained clock to vendor sustained clock target via nvidia-smi --applications-clocks (driver-backed profile).
- H100: start with power cap 350W; for microburst-heavy services leave power cap at default but restrict max boost if VRM temps > 75C.
- L4: use default power mode; if throttling observed, enforce p-state 0 (lowest latency) and reduce concurrent batches.
- MI300: use ROCm recommended perf profile; avoid manual overclocking. If memory fragmentation observed, schedule periodic process restarts to defragment HBM allocation.

Kernel selection guidance (runtime):
- Prefer fused attention / MVF kernel implementations for long sequences when they exist. Monitor kernel fallback rates.
- Expose a runtime flag: --kernel-preference=[fast-smallseq|fast-longseq|memory-saver]. For short queries bias toward fast-smallseq kernels even if memory footprint increases.
- Instrument and log per-request kernel variant id (small integer) to correlate latency spikes to kernel fallback paths.

KV cache sizing & eviction rules (practical ops):
- Baseline: retain KV cache only for authenticated session requests where future requests likely to reference previous context (chat). For non-chat batch workloads, set kv_retention=off to free memory.
- Per-GPU reservation: reserve a KV slab (rounded up to 1GB) per active model instance to avoid fragmentation during rolling restarts.
- Eviction policy: LRU with time-based TTL (default 60s). For bursty workloads use adaptive TTL: if request rate drops below 20% of peak for a model, reduce TTL to 15s to reclaim memory.
- Transparent fallback: when KV cannot be allocated, runtime should log a specific event (KV_ALLOC_FAIL) and fall back to stateless decode mode for that request rather than OOM-killing the worker.

Scheduling knobs and heuristics:
- Microburst handling: keep a small headroom pool of GPUs in each rack pinned at slightly higher clocks to absorb burst traffic; routing layer should detect burst start and prefer these nodes until KV warmup completes.
- Batch sizing heuristics: batch size by tokens not by request count; cap max tokens per batch to avoid long tail latencies.
- Co-location rules: do not colocate KV-heavy models with large serving models on same GPU unless memory headroom >= 25%.

Measurement recipe (what to collect quickly):
- Per-request: p50/p95/p99 latency, kernel_variant, kv_hit/miss, allocated_kv_bytes, gpu_util_pct, sm_efficiency, mem_used, mem_total, power_draw_W, gpu_temp_C, vrm_temp_C if available.
- Aggregate (1m/5m): kernel_fallback_rate, kv_alloc_fail_rate, OOM_events, context_switch_rate.
- SLOs: alert if p99 latency increases >20% vs rolling baseline or kv_alloc_fail_rate > 0.1% for 5m.

Commands and quick checks (examples):
- NVIDIA: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu,clocks.sm,clocks.gr,clocks.mem,power.draw,memory.used,memory.total --format=csv -l 2
- Check kernel fallback in runtime logs: grep "kernel_fallback" /var/log/redwood/runtime/*.log | tail -n 200
- KV slab usage (example endpoint exposed by runtime): curl -s http://localhost:9900/metrics | grep kv_slab_used_bytes
- ROCm example: rocminfo && rocm-smi --showtemp --showpower --showclkinfo

Experiment plan (safe progression):
1) Canary job: pick 2 nodes per rack; increase sustained clock by +5% on A100 only; run steady QPS workload and microburst script for 6 hours. Collect metrics and look for thermal/VRM excursions or kernel_fallback increase.
2) Power cap sweep: for a representative model, sweep power caps in -10% steps from default down to -40% and measure p99 and token cost. Identify knee point where p99 rises >10%.
3) KV TTL sensitivity: run chat workload with TTLs [15s,30s,60s,120s] and measure memory pressure and kv_hit_rate.
4) Kernel preference validation: test fast-longseq vs fast-smallseq with a mixed distribution of sequence lengths; compute per-model p95 and kernel_fallback_rate.

Safety, rollback, and escalation:
- Always run changes on canary subset first. If p99 latency regresses >15% or if GPU temp > 85C sustained for 5m, immediately revert clocks/power caps.
- If adjustments cause OOMs: set kv_retention=off and restart worker; revert clocking changes. File incident RNW-#### and notify eng-sre and perf team.

Operational checklist (on-call quick steps):
- Step 0: Confirm symptoms (latency vs cost, which model/service).
- Step 1: Check per-request flags: kernel_variant, kv_hit, mem_used.
- Step 2: nvidia-smi / rocm-smi snapshot and look for temp/power spikes.
- Step 3: If VRM/thermal problem: reduce boost/clock to vendor sustained levels and route traffic to spare nodes.
- Step 4: If KV allocation failures: lower kv_retention for that model and schedule a graceful restart of workers during low-traffic window.
- Step 5: After remediation, run a short controlled traffic replay against canaries to validate.

Open questions and follow-ups (todo):
- Should we expose per-model adaptive power cap controller (auto-scale power within thermal envelope) in runtime? Prototype required. Owner: Diego Ramos.
- Better telemetry for VRM temps across vendors — current fleet misses VRM on H100s. Action: Mei Lin to open vendor support ticket.
- Evaluate MI300 kernel parity: create a compatibility matrix of kernels we use on CUDA vs ROCm. Owner: Jonah Brooks.

Notes to self (short commands & links):
- Microburst simulator: scripts/perf/microburst_runner.py --qps-top=500 --burst-duration=10s
- Local telemetry query: curl -s http://localhost:9900/debug/kv | jq .
- Relevant PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/789

Last experiment log (quick):
- 2025-01-22 canary A100 +5% sustained clocks: p99 -2.6%, but VRM temp climbed 10C and minor kernel_fallback events observed under 95th percentile sequences. Reverted to sustained baseline; flagged to perf for longer microburst window tests.

If you edit this doc: append short note at bottom with date/name and link to run id (we use RNW-run-<date>). Keep content minimal and pragmatic.

- Aisha
